props.title: Five
props.initialSlug: Nuclear war leaves only five survivors in L.A.

sections.content: **Five (1951)** (1951) stands as one of the earliest and most influential post-apocalyptic films, blazing a trail that later classics like The World, The Flesh and the Devil (1959) and The Last Man on Earth (1964) would follow. Director Arch Oboler crafted this stark survival tale with just five characters - the only survivors of a nuclear catastrophe. Shot in a stark black-and-white that emphasizes the emptiness of their world, the film confronts racial tensions and human nature stripped to its essence. Its influence echoes through **The Quiet Earth** (1985) and **Night of the Comet** (1984).

sections.content: The atomic anxiety that powers **Five** (1951) emerged from very real Cold War fears, spawning a wave of nuclear nightmare films. Panic in Year Zero! (1962) follows a family fleeing Los Angeles after a nuclear strike, while **The Day the Earth Caught Fire** (1961) imagines global catastrophe from nuclear testing. These films share **Five's** focus on human dynamics under extreme pressure, though few match its intimate scale.

What sets **Five** (1951) apart is its groundbreaking production approach. Shot largely at Oboler's Frank Lloyd Wright-designed house, it creates apocalyptic devastation through suggestion rather than spectacle. This minimalist technique influenced later films like The Last Man on Earth (1964) and **Night of the Comet** (1984), proving how effective implied destruction could be. sections.content: The DNA of **Five** (1951) runs through countless later films. Its basic premise - survivors thrown together after catastrophe - became a template for everything from **The Ultimate Warrior** (1975) to **28 Days Later** (2002). Its exploration of racial tension amid apocalypse particularly influenced films like The World, The Flesh and the Devil (1959) and elements of **Night of the Living Dead** (1968).
